interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the part's name change when you flip, empty or add one mark on the circle: pump to motor, oil to air, fixed to variable.
interactive.title: The symbol kit
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. The main picture is a kit of fluid power marks, drawn to the international standard. A tray along the top holds the marks, each with a small label saying what it means. A large circle is usually a machine that turns. A solid triangle is oil, pointing the way it flows. An empty triangle is air, pointing the same way. A slanted arrow means the part can be adjusted. A zigzag is a spring. A diamond is a part that treats the fluid. A square is one position of a valve. A long box with a piston and its rod is a cylinder. A solid line is a working line. It carries the main flow. A dashed line is a pilot line or a drain. A circle with the letter M is an electric motor. Below the tray is the build area. It holds a circle, with a working line in at the bottom and out at the top. Three switches sit above it. Triangle is Out or In. Fill is Solid or Empty. Arrow is Off or On. On a puzzle the switches keep their place but stay hidden until a right answer. Then they fade in. The triangle sits inside the circle, against the line it points along. Pointing out, its point touches the circle. Pointing in, its flat side does. The rule. Out means the fluid leaves the circle. Something drives the part, so it is a pump, or for air a compressor. In means the fluid enters and turns it, so it is a motor. Solid means oil, and empty means air. The arrow is drawn across the circle. It makes the part adjustable, so a pump's volume per turn can be changed. The part's name is written in words under it. The name changes the moment a switch changes. The three switches give one of eight names, from Hydraulic pump, fixed, to Air motor, variable. A Turn button rotates the built symbol a quarter-turn on each tap. The name stays the same. A Cutaway switch shows a sketch beside the symbol. It is set to Gear or Piston. Gear shows a gear pump. Two meshing gears sit in a casing. They carry oil round the outside, in the spaces between their teeth, from the port marked In at the bottom to the port marked Out at the top. Piston shows a piston pump. A ring of pistons in a turning barrel presses against a fixed tilted plate. The symbol under the sketch does not change. Lower down is a shelf of six finished symbols. A tank is an open-topped box. A double-acting cylinder is a long box with a piston and its rod. A filter is a diamond with a dashed line across it. A cooler is a diamond with a line across it and two arrowheads pointing out. An accumulator is an upright capsule. A pressure gauge is a small circle with a pointer arrow inside it. The pointer stays inside the circle, while an adjusting arrow crosses the whole part. Beside them are six cards, each saying what a part does. The cards read: holds the oil; pushes and pulls a load; cleans the oil; takes heat out of the oil; stores oil under pressure; shows the pressure. Drag a symbol onto its card. A right match sticks and names it. A wrong one slides back. The kit opens with the triangle out, solid, and no arrow. It is named Hydraulic pump, fixed. At phone width the switches and buttons wrap onto two rows, with no word split. The tray wraps onto two rows too. The shelf sits above its cards. Every label is at least 12 px and stays readable at 360 px. Screen by screen. Screen 1, do, typed, Still there?: a hydraulic jack, drawn as a small piston and a big one joined by oil. "A jack's small piston has an area of 10 cm². Its big piston has an area of 200 cm². You push the small one down with 100 N. What load can the big one hold up?" A typed answer: 2000, in N, a whole number. Slips: 5, "That is the areas upside down. The big piston feels the bigger force."; 100, "The pressure is the same on both pistons. The force is pressure times area, so the big one gets more."; 20, "That is the areas' ratio. Multiply your push by it." Hint: "Find the oil's pressure from the small piston, then use it on the big one." Why: 100 N on 10 cm² makes 10 N on every square centimetre. The oil carries that pressure to all 200 cm² of the big piston. So the big piston holds up 2000 N. A right answer says "Still there. The jack's small piston is a simple pump. The symbol now in its place is how a drawing marks a pump." After Check, the jack fades and the kit appears. Screen 2, show, Built from marks: the kit as it opens. Words: "A fluid power symbol is built from a few marks. Each mark means one thing. A large circle is usually a machine that turns. A solid triangle is oil, pointing the way it flows. Oil flowing out of the circle makes it a pump." The tray's marks light in turn. Then the circle and the outward solid triangle join in the build area, named Hydraulic pump, fixed. Read: a circle and a solid triangle pointing out of it, named Hydraulic pump, fixed. Still: the end of the sweep. Screen 3, do, Flip it: the kit with the triangle pointing in. "The triangle now points into the circle. What is the part?" Choices: Hydraulic pump; Hydraulic motor (right); Air motor. Hint on Hydraulic pump: "The triangle shows the way the oil goes. Here it flows into the circle." Hint on Air motor: "The triangle is solid, so this part runs on oil." Why: oil flowing in turns the shaft, so the part is a motor. In a pump the triangle's point touches the circle. In a motor its flat side does. After Check, the Triangle switch flips Out and back In, and the name follows. Screen 4, show, Empty means air: the kit as it opens. Words: "An empty triangle means air instead of oil. Pointing out, it makes a compressor. Pointing in, it makes an air motor." Then "Tap Empty." Read: the Fill switch on Empty, and the empty triangle pointing out, named Air compressor, fixed. Still: Fill on Empty. Screen 5, do, typed, Count the air: a tray of five symbols, in a row that wraps at phone width: a hydraulic pump, an air motor, a hydraulic motor, an air compressor and a variable hydraulic pump. "How many of these five parts run on air?" A typed answer: 2, a whole number. Slips: 3, "Pointing out means a pump. The fill tells oil from air, so count the empty triangles."; 1, "The air motor counts too. Its empty triangle points in." Hint: "Only an empty triangle means air. Count those." Why: the air motor and the compressor have empty triangles. The other three have solid ones, so they run on oil. After Check, the two air parts are ringed. Screen 6, show, The adjusting arrow: the kit as it opens. Words: "A slanted arrow across a part means it can be adjusted. Across a pump, it means the volume each turn delivers can be changed." Then "Tap On." Read: the Arrow switch on, the arrow across the circle, named Hydraulic pump, variable. Still: Arrow on. Screen 7, do, Build one: the kit as it opens. "Which marks make an air motor you can adjust?" Choices: Circle, empty triangle in, slanted arrow (right); Circle, solid triangle in, slanted arrow; Circle, empty triangle out, slanted arrow. Hint on the solid triangle: "A solid triangle means oil. Air is drawn empty." Hint on the triangle out: "Pointing out makes a compressor. A motor's triangle points in." Why: air is the empty triangle. A motor's triangle points in. The arrow makes it adjustable. After Check, the kit is set to it, named Air motor, variable. Screen 8, show, Same symbol, any build: the kit as it opens, with the cutaway beside it. Words: "The symbol says what a part does, not how it is built. A gear pump and a piston pump are nothing alike inside. If each delivers a fixed volume each turn, both take this one symbol." Then "Switch the cutaway between Gear and Piston." Read: a gear pump's cutaway and a piston pump's, side by side, both above the same hydraulic pump symbol. Still: both cutaways shown. Screen 9, do, What it tells you: a lone hydraulic pump symbol, its outlet line drawn upward. "What does this symbol tell you about the real pump?" Choices: It is a gear pump; It pumps oil, a fixed volume each turn (right); Its outlet is on its top. Hint on It is a gear pump: "A gear pump and a piston pump take the same symbol." Hint on Its outlet is on its top: "A symbol shows what is joined, not where the ports sit on the part." Why: the solid triangle pointing out makes it a hydraulic pump. No arrow means fixed. How it is built and where its ports sit come from the part or its data sheet. After Check, the cutaway switches through both pumps under the one symbol. Screen 10, show, The rest of the kit: the shelf of finished symbols. Words: "Other parts use the same marks. A diamond treats the fluid. A dashed line across it makes a filter. Arrowheads pointing out of it make a cooler. A box with a piston and rod is a cylinder. An open-topped box is the tank. An upright capsule stores oil under pressure. A small circle with a pointer inside is a gauge." Then "Drag each symbol onto what it does." Read: the six finished symbols each matched to its card: tank, cylinder, filter, cooler, accumulator and pressure gauge. Still: all six matched. Screen 11, do, Turned on its side: two filters on one sheet, one upright and one turned on its side. "These two symbols sit on one sheet. What are they?" Choices: Two filters (right); A filter and a cooler; Two different parts, as they face different ways. Hint on A filter and a cooler: "A cooler's diamond has arrowheads pointing out. Both of these have a dashed line across." Hint on Two different parts: "Turning a symbol does not change what it is. Look at the marks inside." Why: both are diamonds with a dashed line across, so both are filters. Most symbols mean the same however they are turned on the sheet. A tank and the lines into it are the exception, and stay as drawn. After Check, Turn rotates the second to match the first. Screen 12, do, mixed, Read the power unit: a small power unit: a tank, a filter, an electric motor joined by a shaft to a circle with a solid triangle pointing out and a slanted arrow across it, and a pressure gauge. "What is the circle the electric motor drives?" Choices: A fixed hydraulic pump; A variable hydraulic pump (right); A variable air compressor; A variable hydraulic motor. Hint on A fixed hydraulic pump: "Look across the circle. The slanted arrow means it can be adjusted." Hint on A variable air compressor: "The triangle is solid, so it pumps oil." Hint on A variable hydraulic motor: "The triangle points out. Oil leaves this circle." Why: solid means oil, and out means it pumps. The arrow makes it adjustable. So the electric motor drives a variable hydraulic pump. The small circle on the line out is a gauge. Its pointer stays inside it, while the adjusting arrow crosses the whole pump. After Check, each mark of the pump lights in turn. Screen 13, do, mixed, typed, Count the pumps: one sheet with five circles: an electric motor, a fixed hydraulic pump drawn upright, a variable hydraulic pump turned on its side, a hydraulic motor and a pressure gauge. "How many of the circles on this sheet are pumps?" A typed answer: 2, a whole number. Slips: 1, "The pump turned on its side still counts. Turning a symbol does not change it."; 3, "One of your three is not a pump. The circle with M moves no oil. A motor's triangle points in."; 4, "Only a circle with a triangle pointing out is a pump. The small circle is a gauge. Its pointer stays inside it, and it has no triangle."; 5, "The circle with M is an electric motor. The gauge has no triangle at all." Hint: "Count only the circles with a triangle pointing out." Why: the upright pump and the pump on its side have triangles pointing out. The hydraulic motor's points in. The electric motor and the gauge have none. So 2 are pumps. After Check, the two pumps are ringed.
interactive.ignores: The kit holds only a few of the marks in use. Real symbols add more. A curved arrow shows a shaft's turning direction. Two triangles mark a part that runs both ways. A box of long dashes and dots goes round parts built as one unit. The cutaways are simple sketches, not to scale. A real piston pump has more parts. The switches give each name in two words, fixed or variable. Real data sheets say much more. Makers and older standards draw a few symbols a little differently. Where a sheet's own legend differs, the legend wins.

explain.text:
A fluid power symbol is built from a few simple marks. Each mark means one thing. So you read a symbol mark by mark. That way you can name a part you have never seen drawn. Hydraulic and air diagrams share the same marks, so one skill reads both.

Start with the large circle. It is usually a machine that turns, such as a pump or a motor. A gauge is a smaller circle with a pointer inside it. A triangle inside the large circle, against one of its lines, is an arrowhead for the flow. A solid triangle means oil, and an empty one means air. If the triangle points out along a line, the fluid leaves the circle there. Something drives the shaft and pushes the fluid out, so the part is a pump. If it points in, the fluid enters and turns the shaft, so the part is a motor. In a pump the point of the triangle touches the circle. In a motor its flat side does.[^1] An air pump is called a compressor. So an empty triangle pointing out is a compressor. A slanted arrow across the circle means the part can be adjusted. It crosses the whole circle, while a gauge's pointer stays inside its own. On a pump, it means you can change the volume of fluid each turn delivers. That volume is the pump's [[displacement]]. So three marks on the circle, each drawn one of two ways, name eight different machines.

The lines and other shapes work the same way. A solid line is a [[working line]]. It carries the main flow. A dashed line is a [[pilot line]] or a drain. A pilot line carries a small flow that signals or moves another part. A drain carries leakage back to the tank. A zigzag is a spring. A diamond is a part that treats the fluid. A dashed line across it makes a filter. A long box with a piston and its rod is a cylinder. Drawn plain, it is double-acting, so oil pushes it both ways. With a spring inside at one end, it is single-acting. Oil pushes it one way, and the spring brings it back. A square is one position of a valve.

A symbol shows what a part does, not how it is built.[^2] You trace a circuit by what each part does to the flow. Drawing the build would only crowd the sheet. A gear pump and a piston pump are nothing alike inside. If each delivers a fixed volume each turn, both take the same symbol. Nor does a symbol show where the ports sit on the real part, or which way up it is fitted. Most symbols mean the same however they are turned on the sheet. A tank and the lines into it are the exception, and stay as drawn.[^3] So the nameplate or data sheet tells you how a part is built. The symbol tells you its job. **Each mark in a fluid power symbol means one thing. So you can read a symbol you have never met, mark by mark, as what the part does.**

analogy.text: You already read electrical symbols this way. A resistor with a slanted arrow across it is a variable resistor. A diode with two small arrows pointing away from it is an LED, which gives out light. Each added mark changes one thing about the part. Fluid power symbols work the same way. The slanted arrow even means the same thing: adjustable.
analogy.breaks: The same shape can mean different things on the two kinds of sheet. On a circuit diagram a circle with a cross is a lamp. On a fluid power sheet a circle with a triangle is a pump or a motor. So check which kind of sheet you hold before you read its marks.

practice.text:
- A symbol never tells you whether a line holds pressure now. An accumulator can hold oil under pressure with the pump stopped. Before you open anything, isolate, vent and prove the pressure gone by the plant's procedure.
- Check the sheet's legend first. Where it differs from what you expect, the legend wins.
- Find the main shape. A large circle usually turns. A diamond treats the fluid. A long box is a cylinder, and a square is a valve position.
- Read the marks one at a time. Solid triangle or empty, pointing out or in, arrow or none, spring or none.
- Put the meanings together into a name, such as variable hydraulic pump.
- For how the part is built, read its nameplate or data sheet, not the symbol.
- Find it on the plant by its tag, never by its look or where it sits.

**Rule of thumb:** triangle out, a pump. Triangle in, a motor. Empty, air. Arrow across, adjustable.

**Worked example:** a power unit shows a circle with M, joined by a shaft to a second circle. The second circle has a solid triangle pointing out and a slanted arrow across it. The circle with M is an electric motor. The second circle is a machine that turns. Its solid triangle means oil. Pointing out means the oil leaves it, so it is a pump. The arrow means it can be adjusted. So an electric motor drives a variable hydraulic pump. The symbol does not say whether it is a piston pump or another kind. The nameplate does.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading the triangle's direction backwards, and taking a pump for a motor.
- Taking an empty triangle for oil. Empty means air.
- Missing the slanted arrow, and reading a variable pump as fixed.
- Reading the symbol as the part's shape, or as where its ports sit.
- Taking a symbol turned on its side for a different part.
- Taking the circle with M, the electric motor, for a pump.
